problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=7{t}^{2}+5{t}^{4}{e}^{t}$ for $s>1.$

activity_context.topic_title: The First Shifting Theorem of Laplace Transforms

feedback.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094645/assets/82d01729627b5871739120d2e512cf54610eaaf43f6f2f2c454b7e39803937a2.png)

Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the graph of the Laplace transform $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $L{{e}^{-2t}f(t)}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L{{e}^{-2t}f(t)},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $2$ units to the left.
